title: Threat models and drills

story: Four weeks ago, while the agent platform was still a design, the team wrote down a promise: a sandbox VM can reach only the package mirror, nothing else on the internet. Since then dozens of changes have landed. One engineer opened a route "for an hour" to download a tool. Another changed the proxy's settings to fix a slow build. Every change was reviewed, and every change looked harmless on its own.

Next week Nova, our ticket-to-PR agent, starts working on real tickets. Is the promise still true? Nobody knows, because nobody has tried to break it since it was written. And if someone did break it, a prompt injection pulling data out for example, would anyone even notice?
hook.question: How do we know the walls are really there, and that someone would notice an attempt to get through them?

read.h: Write the risks down as rows
p: A threat model is a written list of what can go wrong with a system and what we do about each thing. The classic way to build one is four questions: what are we working on, what can go wrong, what are we going to do about it, and did we do a good job? For agents, the second question has a ready answer from the lesson on the lethal trifecta: go through each part of the platform (the VM, the broker, the gateway, the proxy, the orchestrator, the Slack app) and ask where untrusted text gets in, what private data it could reach, and how it could get out.

Each answer becomes one row with four parts: the risk, the leg it touches, the wall or the guidance that handles it, and an owner, the one person or team who answers for it. Writing "guidance" in a row is allowed and honest: it says the risk is reduced, not stopped. What is not allowed is a risk with no row, or a row with no owner. The session also forces open decisions to close. Should github.com be on the proxy list? The answer was no, because git and the GitHub API already go through the broker, and an open github.com would be one more way for data to leave.

code.text:
| Risk | Leg | Wall or guidance | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ticket or Slack text tells Nova to leak or break something | untrusted input | wall: no keys in the VM; egress allow-list | Platform |
| A sandbox reaches a site that is not on the list | way out | wall: proxy allow-list, no other route out, DNS firewall | DevOps |
| CI runs an agent's branch with CI's own secrets | way out | wall: narrow CI's secret access before agents push | Platform, DevOps |
| The docker group is root on the VM | private data | wall: the VM's cloud role holds almost nothing | DevOps |
| The run's capability is visible in the command history | private data | guidance: it expires with the run; few people can read it | Security |
| github.com on the proxy list | way out | decision: no; git and the GitHub API go through the broker | Security |

notes.text: The attack from the trifecta lesson, with the walls that make it harmless.
The promise from the story. The lab probes exactly this row.
Guidance, said honestly: this risk is smaller, not gone.
A decision is a row too, with its reason, so nobody reopens it by accident.

read.h: Probe: try it from where the attacker stands
p: Designs drift while they are built, so a few weeks later the runtime is reviewed again as built. Someone from Security first reads the real configuration: the VM's cloud role, the network rules, the proxy list, the broker's scopes and the GitHub App's permissions. Then come the probes. A probe is a small, harmless attempt, made from inside a real sandbox, to do one thing a wall forbids: reach a site that is not on the list, read the cloud metadata service (the address that hands an AWS machine its role's credentials), find a token in the environment, push to main, use another run's capability.

Every probe has two pass conditions, not one. The attempt must fail, and it must leave a trace: a log line, a refused-actions entry, or an alert. A wall that holds silently is only half a wall, because the next attacker will keep trying until one attempt works, and nobody will know they are trying. Our proxy, for example, writes every denied request to the logs, and more than five denied requests from one machine in five minutes raise an alert to the alerts channel and to Security.

code.file: probes.sh (the lab version; the real probes run in a sandbox VM)
code.text:
#!/bin/sh
# Each probe tries one thing. PASS means the sandbox behaved the way the threat model says.
failed=0
refused() { if "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "FAIL  $name: it worked"; failed=1; else echo "PASS  $name: refused"; fi; }
works() { if "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "PASS  $name: works"; else echo "FAIL  $name: broken"; failed=1; fi; }

name="package mirror via the proxy"; works   curl -sf --max-time 10 https://registry.npmjs.org/
name="github.com via the proxy";     refused curl -sf --max-time 5 https://github.com
name="github.com around the proxy";  refused curl -sf --max-time 5 --noproxy '*' https://github.com
name="cloud metadata service";       refused curl -sf --max-time 3 --noproxy '*' http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
name="token in the environment";     refused sh -c 'env | grep -qiE "token|secret|_key="'
exit $failed

notes.text: A probe that must work: frustrated people disable walls that break the real job.
Through the proxy: refused, and the proxy writes a DENIED line.
Around the proxy: refused only if the sandbox has no other route out.
169.254.169.254 is the cloud metadata service. A sandbox must never get role credentials from it.

p: Probes test the walls. Failure drills test the recovery: they cause a failure on purpose during a test run, with a drill ticket, and check that the platform does what the playbook, the written plan for each kind of failure, says it will do. Kill the VM in the middle of a run, and the run must continue on a fresh VM from the last checkpoint. Kill it twice, and the run must stop and tell a person. Make the gateway answer "overloaded" for twenty minutes, and the run must pause and then continue. Give Nova a ticket that asks it to edit a CI workflow, and the edit must be refused and listed in the PR.

A playbook nobody has tested is a guess, and scripts make the drills repeatable after every big change. Our drills are node:test files that act on the real platform, so they never run in CI. VM failures use AWS Fault Injection Service (FIS), an AWS service that runs experiments such as "terminate this instance". The whole kit is run with Security before the pilot. A drill that fails and touches a wall blocks the pilot: walls are fixed before real tickets arrive, not after.

notes.text: A drill ticket with a small, known fix, and timers in minutes instead of days.
An AWS FIS experiment kills the machine, as a real failure would.
Nothing was lost: the last checkpoint is on the branch.
The trace: the dead-VM metric went up, so the alert would fire.

read.h: The runbook: written for the tired person
p: Every alert links to a runbook: the steps to follow when it fires. Write it for someone who is tired, stressed and has never seen this part of the platform, because that is who reads it at 3 AM. One action per line, in the order to do them, and each line says what to click or type and what you should see. The goal for this one is plain: anyone on call can stop a misbehaving agent within a minute.

After the drills, the runbook gets one more thing: what each failure looks like in Slack, in Grafana and in the logs, taken from the drill that caused it. A runbook written before anything was broken is as much a guess as an untested playbook.

code.text:
## Find the run
1. Open the ticket's Slack thread. The status message names the run, e.g. nova:RH-1234.
2. Or search the Temporal UI for that workflow ID.
3. For a blocked-egress alert: find the VM by its private IP, then its run-id tag.

## Stop one run
1. Press Stop on the status message. You should see "Stopped" and "VM released".

## Stop every run of an agent
1. Turn on that agent's kill switch. No new runs start.
2. Send the stop signal to its running workflows as one batch.

## Cut its model access
1. Revoke the agent's key at the gateway. Its next model call fails.

notes.text: Start from where the person already is: the Slack thread the alert points to.
Every step says what you should see, so the reader knows it worked.
The kill switch makes new starts fail, so nothing new begins while you clean up.

lab.title: Probe a sealed sandbox, then break a wall on purpose
needs: About 100 MB for the curl and Node images
lab.goal: Build a small sandbox network with an egress proxy, probe it until every wall holds and leaves a trace, then break a wall in a drill and write the threat-model row.

guess.q: A probe from the sandbox tries to reach github.com without the proxy, and it fails. The proxy's log shows nothing about it. Is that a good result?

options.text: Yes: the attempt failed, which is all a wall has to do.
options.why: It held, but a wall that holds silently lets an attacker keep trying with nobody watching.

options.text: No: it should have succeeded, because github.com is a normal site.
options.why: github.com is off the list on purpose; git and the GitHub API go through the broker.

options.text: Half: the wall held, but this attempt left no trace, so another layer must log it.
options.why: Every probe must fail and be seen. An attempt around the proxy never reaches the proxy, so the network itself must record it, which in AWS means flow logs and the DNS firewall.

follow.say: Make a folder and write the egress proxy. It allows HTTPS to one site, which stands for our package mirror, and writes one line for every request, allowed or denied.
Write the probes. Four must be refused and one must work, because frustrated people disable a wall that breaks the real job.
follow.do:
cat > probes.sh <<'EOF'
#!/bin/sh
# Each probe tries one thing. PASS means the sandbox behaved the way the threat model says.
failed=0
refused() { if "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "FAIL  $name: it worked"; failed=1; else echo "PASS  $name: refused"; fi; }
works() { if "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "PASS  $name: works"; else echo "FAIL  $name: broken"; failed=1; fi; }

name="package mirror via the proxy"; works   curl -sf --max-time 10 https://registry.npmjs.org/
name="github.com via the proxy";     refused curl -sf --max-time 5 https://github.com
name="github.com around the proxy";  refused curl -sf --max-time 5 --noproxy '*' https://github.com
name="cloud metadata service";       refused curl -sf --max-time 3 --noproxy '*' http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/
name="token in the environment";     refused sh -c 'env | grep -qiE "token|secret|_key="'
exit $failed
EOF

follow.say: Build the network. lab-sandbox is internal, so containers on it have no route to the internet. The proxy lives on lab-open, which has internet, and is also connected to lab-sandbox, so it is the sandbox's only way out.
follow.do:
docker network create --internal lab-sandbox
docker network create lab-open
docker run -d --name lab-proxy --network lab-open -v "$PWD":/lab:ro node:24-bookworm-slim node /lab/proxy.mjs
docker network connect lab-sandbox lab-proxy
sleep 1 && docker logs lab-proxy
follow.see:
5c1e…(three long IDs, different on your machine)
proxy listening on 3128

follow.say: Probe the sealed sandbox: a container on lab-sandbox only, with the proxy set the way the VM's environment sets it.
follow.do: docker run --rm -i --network lab-sandbox -e HTTPS_PROXY=http://lab-proxy:3128 --entrypoint sh curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -s < probes.sh; echo "exit $?"
follow.see:
PASS  package mirror via the proxy: works
PASS  github.com via the proxy: refused
PASS  github.com around the proxy: refused
PASS  cloud metadata service: refused
PASS  token in the environment: refused
exit 0

follow.say: Now check the second condition, the trace. Which of the four refused attempts can you find in the proxy's log?
follow.see:
proxy listening on 3128
2026-10-15T23:17:07.097Z ALLOWED ::ffff:172.22.0.3 CONNECT registry.npmjs.org:443
2026-10-15T23:17:07.163Z DENIED ::ffff:172.22.0.3 CONNECT github.com:443

follow.say: The drill: break two walls on purpose, the way a hurried change would. Start the sandbox on lab-open, which has its own route out, and put a token in its environment.
follow.do: docker run --rm -i --network lab-open -e HTTPS_PROXY=http://lab-proxy:3128 -e GITHUB_TOKEN=ghs_FAKE --entrypoint sh curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -s < probes.sh; echo "exit $?"
follow.see:
PASS  package mirror via the proxy: works
PASS  github.com via the proxy: refused
FAIL  github.com around the proxy: it worked
PASS  cloud metadata service: refused
FAIL  token in the environment: it worked
exit 1

follow.say: Write what the drill found as threat-model rows, with a wall and an owner each, so it cannot be forgotten.
follow.do:
cat > threat-model.md <<'EOF'
| Risk | Leg | Wall or guidance | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| A sandbox gets a route around the proxy | way out | wall: sandbox subnets have no route out; probe it after every network change | DevOps |
| A token in the sandbox environment | private data | wall: no keys in the VM; the broker holds them | Platform |
EOF
cat threat-model.md
follow.see:
| Risk | Leg | Wall or guidance | Owner |
|---|---|---|---|
| A sandbox gets a route around the proxy | way out | wall: sandbox subnets have no route out; probe it after every network change | DevOps |
| A token in the sandbox environment | private data | wall: no keys in the VM; the broker holds them | Platform |

lab.build: A prompt injection that wants data out usually tries many times. Make the trace useful: write alert.mjs, which reads the proxy log on stdin and prints an ALERT line for every source with more than 5 DENIED requests in the last 5 minutes (the time is the first word of each line, the verdict the second, the source the third), or "no alert". Check it with docker logs lab-proxy 2>&1 | node alert.mjs, then play the injected agent: docker run --rm --network lab-sandbox -e HTTPS_PROXY=http://lab-proxy:3128 --entrypoint sh curlimages/curl:8.11.1 -c 'for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6; do curl -s -o /dev/null https://github.com; done' and run the alert again. Finish by cleaning up: docker rm -f lab-proxy && docker network rm lab-sandbox lab-open.
checks: The sealed sandbox prints five PASS lines and exit 0.
The proxy log has an ALLOWED line for the mirror and a DENIED line for github.com, and nothing for the attempt around the proxy.
The drill prints two FAIL lines and exit 1.
threat-model.md has one row for each FAIL, each with a wall and an owner.
alert.mjs says no alert before the loop and prints an ALERT line for the sandbox's address after it.
docker ps and docker network ls no longer show lab-proxy, lab-sandbox or lab-open.
lab.fix: Someone made the probe script "less noisy" by changing refused() so it prints PASS whatever happens: if "$@" >/dev/null 2>&1; then echo "PASS  $name: refused"; fi. Make that change and run the drill again: it now reports nothing wrong, although the token is in the environment. A probe that cannot fail is worse than no probe, because it gives false comfort. Restore refused() and prove it can fail by running the drill once more.
explain: What two conditions must every probe meet, and why is the second one needed?
Why did the attempt around the proxy leave no line in the proxy's log, and where would the real platform see it?
What makes a runbook usable at 3 AM by someone who has never seen the platform?
lab.done: The sealed sandbox passed every probe, the drill failed where it should, each finding has a row with an owner, the alert fired, and you removed the container and both networks.

check.q: A threat-model row says: "Risk: CI runs an agent's branch with CI's secrets. Wall or guidance: (empty). Owner: (empty)." What is wrong?

options.text: Nothing; the risk is written down, which is the point
options.why: A risk without a wall or guidance and without an owner is a worry, not a plan. Nobody will act on it.

options.text: It needs a wall or an honest "guidance", and one owner who answers for it
options.why: Every row says what handles the risk and who owns it. "Guidance" is allowed; an empty cell is not.

options.text: CI risks do not belong in an agent threat model
options.why: They do: an agent's branch runs CI with CI's secrets, so it is a way out for the agent.

check.q: Why do the failure drills never run in CI's npm test?

options.text: They are too slow for CI
options.why: Some are slow, but the real reason is what they touch.

options.text: Because CI has no network access
options.why: CI can reach the network. That is not the reason.

options.text: They act on the real platform, killing VMs and starting drill tickets, so they run on purpose, with people watching
options.why: A drill causes a real failure. It runs from npm run drills, by a person, with Security, never as a side effect of a PR.

check.q: A probe from a real sandbox tries to read the cloud metadata service and is refused. Nothing appears in any log. What does the review conclude?

options.text: The wall holds but is silent, so a finding is written: add a trace for that attempt
options.why: Every probe must fail and leave a trace. A silent wall lets an attacker keep trying unseen.
Half a pass. The review checks for the trace as well.

options.text: Fail: the metadata service should answer, so the VM can get its role
options.why: The sandbox's agent user must never get role credentials. Refusing it is right.

p: The threat model lives in docs/threat-model.md in the ai-agents repo. It starts in a half-day session with Security while the runtime is being built (walk the three legs for each part, check each wall, name the soft spots, close the open decisions) and is checked again in the design review before the pilot, which reads the deployed config and probes from a real sandbox as the agent user: IMDS (the cloud metadata service), a blocked site, an unknown domain, a push to main or another repo, another run's capability and artifacts.

The drill kit lives in drills/src/ (vm.ts, agent.ts, outside-services.ts, people.ts) and runs with npm run drills -w drills against the real platform with drill tickets: AWS FIS for VM faults, fixture tickets for agent faults, drill-only switches for outside services. It ends with /nova DRILL-100 going from Slack to a draft PR on the scratch repo, with the blocked-site try visible in VictoriaLogs. Alerts go to #ai-agents-alerts, and the blocked-egress rule fires on more than 5 denied proxy requests from one source in 5 minutes, linking to docs/runbooks/when-an-agent-misbehaves.md.

tickets.why: The threat-model session: legs, walls, soft spots and decisions, written as rows with owners.
The design review: read the deployed config, then probe from a real sandbox; every probe must fail and leave a trace.
The drill kit: one node:test drill per failure, with AWS FIS, fixture tickets and drill-only switches.
Run every drill with Security, fix what fails, and add what each failure looks like to the runbook.
The alerts to #ai-agents-alerts and the misbehaving-agent runbook.
Refused actions listed in the PR, and the blocked-egress alert.

words.plain: A written list of what can go wrong, each as a row with its wall or guidance and an owner.
A small, harmless attempt from inside the sandbox to do something a wall forbids. It must fail and leave a trace.
Causing a failure on purpose in a test run, then checking the platform recovers the way the playbook says.
The steps to follow when an alert fires, one action per line, written for someone who has never seen the system.
The address 169.254.169.254 that gives an AWS machine its role's credentials. Sandboxes must not reach it.

review.q: Write a threat-model row for: "a fooled agent posts a secret into its PR".
review.a: Risk: secret leaks through the PR. Leg: private data (and way out). Wall: no keys in the VM; the broker holds them, and the secret guard blocks responses containing them. Owner: Platform.

review.q: List four probes the design review runs from a real sandbox.
review.a: Read the metadata service's credentials; reach a site not on the list; resolve an unknown domain; push to main or another repo; use another run's capability or artifacts. Each must fail and leave a trace.

review.q: A drill that touches a wall fails a week before the pilot. What happens?
review.a: It blocks the pilot. Small failures are fixed the same day; anything bigger becomes a ticket with an owner, and the pilot waits until the wall holds.

remember: Write every risk as a row with a wall and an owner, then try to break it on purpose: it must fail, and someone must see it fail.
